plan.concept: Scaled dot-product attention: softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V, with editable Q, K, V and a scaling toggle.
learning_outcomes: Compute similarity scores QK^T and see how dividing by sqrt(d_k) changes them.
Convert scores to attention weights with softmax and verify each row sums to 1.
See the output as a weighted average of the value rows.
Explain why scaling matters when d_k is large.
plan.visual_strategy: Pipeline of score -> scaled score -> weights -> output, plus heatmaps of scores and weights, a table of the output rows, and a sweep showing how the largest weight grows with d_k when scaling is off.
plan.misconception: Softmax weights are not a similarity ranking alone: they are a probability distribution over value rows, and without scaling large d_k makes that distribution nearly one-hot.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Step by Step
idea: Attention maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output. Each query is compared with every key by a dot product; after dividing by sqrt(d_k) and applying softmax, the resulting weights say how much of each value row to mix. The output row is the weighted average of the value rows.
why_it_matters: This single formula is the core operation of the Transformer. The 1/sqrt(d_k) factor keeps the softmax in a well-behaved range so gradients do not vanish when the key dimension is large.

equations.caption: Softmax turns each row of scores into weights that sum to 1.
Dot product of one query with one key; its variance grows like d_k when entries are independent with variance 1.

symbols.meaning: matrix of queries, one row per query position; shape n x d_k
matrix of keys, one row per key position; shape m x d_k
matrix of values, one row per key position; shape m x d_v
dimension of each query/key vector (number of columns of Q and K)
dimension of each value vector (number of columns of V)
matrix of raw similarity scores, shape n x m
scaling factor that counteracts the growth of dot-product variance
row-wise normalization into non-negative weights summing to 1
output matrix, shape n x d_v

walkthrough: Form the raw scores S = QK^T: entry (i,j) is the dot product of query row i with key row j.
Divide every score by sqrt(d_k) to get the scaled scores; this keeps their spread roughly constant as d_k grows.
Apply softmax to each row of scaled scores, producing attention weights A whose rows are non-negative and sum to 1.
Multiply A by V: output row i is the weighted average of the value rows, with weights A[i,:].
Inspect the weights: equal scores give a uniform row, a dominant score gives a row concentrated on one value.

explorations.title: Equal scores give uniform weights
explorations.change: Set all three rows of K equal (as in the preset) so every key is identical.
explorations.observe: Every score in row 1 is 2, the weights row becomes [0.333, 0.333, 0.333], and the output row is the plain average of the value rows, [0.667, 0.667].
explorations.why: Softmax of equal scores is uniform, so the output is an unweighted average of V.

explorations.title: A dominant score concentrates attention
explorations.observe: Row 1 scores are [4, 0, 0]; after scaling by sqrt(3) the weights are about [0.834, 0.083, 0.083], so the output row is close to v1 = [1, 0].
explorations.why: A large positive score dominates the softmax, so that value row supplies most of the output.

misconception.title: Common misunderstanding
misconception.text: The attention weights are not the output. They are a probability distribution over the value rows; the output is the weighted average A V. Also, scaling does not change the ranking of scores, only their spread, which is what keeps softmax from saturating.

from_paper: Attention maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where query, keys, values and output are all vectors (Section 3.2).
The output is a weighted sum of the values, with weights from a compatibility function of the query with each key (Section 3.2).
Scaled dot-product attention computes dot products of the query with all keys, divides each by sqrt(d_k), and applies softmax to obtain the weights on the values (Section 3.2.1).
Dot-product attention is identical to the algorithm except for the scaling factor 1/sqrt(d_k) (Section 3.2.1).
For large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing softmax into regions with extremely small gradients; the paper scales by 1/sqrt(d_k) to counteract this (Section 3.2.1).
our_simplifications: We use tiny editable matrices (2 queries, 3 keys, d_k = 3, d_v = 2) instead of the paper's d_k = d_v = 64 and d_model = 512.
We show a single attention head, not the 8-head multi-head attention of Section 3.2.2.
The sweep over d_k is a toy illustration of the variance argument in footnote 1; it is not a paper experiment.
No training, masking, or positional encoding is included.
quotes: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by $\sqrt{d_{k}}$ , and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.
To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}$ .
